clinicalPearls: The CV2 antibody recognises CRMP5 (collapsin response mediator protein 5), which is expressed in adult oligodendrocytes and a subset of neurons.
It is most often associated with small cell lung carcinoma and thymoma.
The phenotype is strikingly heterogeneous, spanning encephalomyelitis, cerebellar ataxia, chorea, cranial neuropathy, myelopathy and a mixed sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy.
Distinctive features that point to CRMP5 include chorea and painless visual loss from optic neuritis or retinitis and uveitis.
The peripheral neuropathy may be demyelinating or axonal and can closely mimic an inflammatory neuropathy.
Anti-CV2/CRMP5 frequently coexists with anti-Hu or anti-amphiphysin, which broadens the clinical picture and the tumour association.
Compared with anti-Hu and anti-Yo disease, a subset of patients shows modest stabilisation or improvement with tumour treatment and immunotherapy.
Olfactory and taste disturbance and subtle visual symptoms can be early, easily overlooked clues.
reference.pathophysiology: CRMP5 is a cytoplasmic phosphoprotein of the collapsin response mediator family involved in axon guidance and neurite outgrowth during development and re-expressed in a restricted pattern in the adult nervous system, including oligodendrocytes and neurons of the basal ganglia, retina and other regions. Ectopic expression by small cell lung carcinoma or thymoma triggers an onconeural immune response in which the antibody serves as a marker while cytotoxic T-cell mechanisms contribute to tissue injury. The wide anatomical distribution of the antigen explains the multifocal disease: basal-ganglia involvement produces chorea, optic nerve and retinal involvement produce visual loss, oligodendrocyte involvement contributes to demyelination, and cerebellar, spinal and peripheral-nerve involvement complete a broad clinical spectrum, accompanied by inflammatory infiltrates and neuronal and glial loss.
additionalDifferentials: Anti-Hu paraneoplastic encephalomyelitis, which may coexist
Huntington disease and other genetic or acquired chorea
Optic neuritis from multiple sclerosis or neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder
Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy or vasculitic neuropathy
Other causes of paraneoplastic or autoimmune retinopathy
Wilson disease or drug-induced movement disorder
additionalInvestigations: Serum and cerebrospinal fluid anti-CV2/CRMP5 with confirmatory immunohistochemistry and line blot, plus a panel for coexisting onconeural antibodies
CT of the chest and whole-body FDG-PET for small cell lung carcinoma
CT or MRI of the anterior mediastinum for thymoma
MRI of the brain and spinal cord for striatal, white-matter or cord signal change
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to characterise the neuropathy
Formal ophthalmological assessment with fundoscopy, optical coherence tomography and electroretinography
Cerebrospinal fluid for pleocytosis, raised protein and oligoclonal bands
redFlags: Subacute painless visual loss from optic neuritis or retinopathy
Occult small cell lung carcinoma or thymoma requiring staging
Thymoma with coexisting myasthenia gravis threatening respiration
reference.prognosis: The outcome is variable and generally guarded, but a subset of patients stabilises or partially improves with early tumour treatment and immunotherapy, more often than in anti-Hu or anti-Yo disease. Prognosis is heavily influenced by the underlying malignancy and any coexisting onconeural antibody.
pitfalls: Attributing chorea to a primary movement disorder and missing the paraneoplastic cause
Overlooking visual symptoms that reflect optic neuritis or retinopathy
Testing for a single antibody and missing coexisting anti-Hu or anti-amphiphysin
Misclassifying the neuropathy as idiopathic chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy
Failing to image the mediastinum for thymoma
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
Consensus diagnostic criteria for paraneoplastic neurological syndromes
management: Treat as a high-risk antineuronal antibody (over 70% cancer association) and urgently search for the underlying small cell lung carcinoma or thymoma rather than pursuing neurologic treatment alone
Run tumor-directed therapy and immunotherapy in parallel, since tumor control alone is less effective in this immune-mediated syndrome
Follow standard histology-specific small cell lung cancer or thymoma staging and treatment pathways for the identified malignancy
If no tumor is found on initial screening, repeat malignancy screening periodically for about two years
Start immunotherapy once viral and bacterial infectious mimics have been reasonably excluded, without waiting for antibody confirmation if clinical suspicion is strong
Use first-line acute options such as corticosteroid pulse therapy, intravenous immunoglobulin, or plasma exchange

For non-responders, consider second-line agents such as rituximab, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, or cyclophosphamide, with tocilizumab as an option in rituximab-refractory autoimmune encephalitis
Expect tumor treatment plus immunotherapy to produce mostly partial stabilization rather than full reversal
Manage chorea symptomatically with dopamine-depleting or antidopaminergic agents when present
Obtain formal ophthalmological assessment and early referral for any visual complaint, given the risk of optic neuritis, retinitis, or uveitis
Support cerebellar ataxia, myelopathy, and peripheral neuropathy with physiotherapy and general supportive care, as these deficits tend to reverse more slowly
Consider testing for coexisting anti-Hu or anti-amphiphysin antibodies at diagnosis, since coexistence can change the tumor association and surveillance needs
Maintain longitudinal tumor surveillance jointly with neurology and oncology and track the neurologic exam serially to judge treatment response
Refer promptly to neuro-oncology or neuro-immunology for coordinated immunotherapy decisions alongside oncology-directed tumor staging and treatment
